Great Scientific American article on why you should not believe the calorie count on food labels.

Disappointing. The most important part of the entire article was at the end:

Processed foods are so easily digested in the stomach and intestines that they give us a lot of energy for very little work. In contrast, veggies, nuts and whole grains make us sweat for our calories, generally offer far more vitamins and nutrients than processed items, and keep our gut bacteria happy. So it would be logical for people who want to eat healthier and cut calories to favor whole and raw foods over highly processed foods.

But all the people who need to know that will have given up reading by then convinced that they're fighting a no-win battle against inaccurate nutrition labeling.

I don't really think so - "cooking" a food counts as processing it as far as this article is concerned. All that does is appeal to the circle jerked idea of "processed = always bad; raw & whole = always good"

Interesting read but I don't think it has much influence on how you should diet.It's not about being exact, but rather about being consistent and patient. Nothing we do in life is 100% optimal but if you make the best effort and adjust/adapt in order to reach your goals then you will be successful. For example, if you aren't losing weight 3-4 weeks in a row, you are not eating at the deficit you thought you were and you need to adjust downward in order to compensate for overeating/underestimating calories.
